title: Jacob, Joseph and the Art of Biblical Narrative
bigQuestion: How does biblical narrative tell so much with so few words, and what do readers gain by reading the Jacob and Joseph stories as literature and as Torah?

story.title: The Man Who Limped at Sunrise
story.kicker: Alone by a river at night, a man fights a stranger until dawn and walks away with a new name.
paragraphs: The river Jabbok runs down to the Jordan from the east. On one night, Genesis 32 says, a man named Jacob sent his wives, his children, his servants and his flocks across the stream and stayed behind alone. He was afraid. His brother Esau, whom he had cheated twenty years before, was coming to meet him with four hundred men. Jacob had prayed, sent gifts ahead, split his camp in two. Now there was nothing left to do but wait for morning.

The text says a man wrestled with him until the break of day. It does not say who the man was. It does not say where he came from. When the stranger saw he could not win, he struck the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and it was strained. Then the stranger asked to be let go, because dawn was breaking. Jacob answered that he would not let go without a blessing. The stranger asked his name. Jacob said it. The stranger told him he would be called Jacob no more, but Israel, because he had striven with God and with men and had prevailed.

Jacob asked the stranger's name. The stranger did not give it. He blessed Jacob and was gone. Jacob named the place Peniel, the face of God, and said he had seen God face to face and lived. The sun rose on him as he passed over, limping. The next verse notes that, because of this, the children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh. A story about one night ends in a rule that Jewish families still keep at the butcher shop.

Who was the stranger? The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. A midrash, followed by Rashi, says he was the guardian angel of Esau. Some modern readers say Jacob wrestled his own conscience, the man he had been, and came out with a new name and a limp. The text supports none of these more than the others. It gives a river, a night, a fight, a wound, a name, a sunrise.

This chapter reads Genesis 25 to 50 as story: how the narrator chooses words, when the narrator stays silent, how a scene repeats with changes, how a single word ties two chapters together. It follows Jacob from the womb to the river to Egypt, and Joseph from his dreams to a palace and a family made whole. At the end, it asks what changes when the same story is read as literature and as Torah.
story.think: The text never names the stranger. What does each reading, angel, Esau's angel, or Jacob's own conscience, do with the fact that Jacob walks away limping?

lessons.title: Economy and Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Biblical narrative tells its stories with very few words about looks, feelings and motives, and that restraint is a technique, not a lack.
reading: Open a novel and you will usually learn what a character looks like, what she is thinking and why she does what she does. Open Genesis 25 and you learn that Esau came out red and hairy, that Jacob held his heel, that Esau hunted and Jacob stayed in tents, and that each parent loved a different son. That is nearly all. The text does not say why Rebekah loved Jacob. It does not say what Jacob felt as he held the heel or the stew. The *narrator*, the voice that tells the story, says almost nothing that a camera could not see.

The literary scholar Robert *Alter*, in The Art of Biblical Narrative (1981), argued that this *economy* is a deliberate art. Hebrew narrative gives the reader actions and speech and holds back judgment. When it does state a motive, as when it says Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his venison, the reason is so small that it becomes a comment. When it gives a physical detail, the detail matters later: Esau's hairiness will be the tool of Jacob's deception in Genesis 27. Nothing is decoration.

The silence puts work on the reader. Was Rebekah right to favor Jacob? Did Esau deserve to lose the blessing? The narrator will not say. Rabbinic readers filled the silence with midrash, sometimes making Esau a villain from the womb and sometimes finding merit in his care for his father. Modern literary readers keep the silence and ask what it does. Both are responses to the same feature: a text that shows and does not tell. Learning to read Genesis means learning to notice what is not on the page and to be careful about what you put there.

words.d: the voice that tells a story; in Genesis it reports actions and speech and rarely states feelings or judgments
in narrative, using the fewest words needed; every detail that is given is meant to count
Robert Alter, American scholar whose The Art of Biblical Narrative (1981) described the literary techniques of the Hebrew Bible

look.title: Two Brothers in Two Verses
look.text: And the boys grew; and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents. Now Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison; and Rebekah loved Jacob.
look.prompt: One parent's love is given a reason and the other's is not. What does the reader learn from the reason that is given, and from the reason that is missing?

check.q: What does the narrator of Genesis usually leave out?
choices: What characters say to each other
check.why: Biblical narrative reports actions, speech and places but rarely states what a character feels or why; Alter calls this its economy.

check.q: Why does the detail that Esau is hairy matter, according to a literary reading?
choices: It shows Esau was the older twin
It becomes the tool of Jacob's deception in Genesis 27
It explains why Isaac loved him
It is a sign that Esau was a shepherd
check.why: In Genesis 27 Jacob wears goat skins so his blind father will feel hair; a physical detail given early is used later, which is typical of the text's economy.

check.q: How do rabbinic midrash and modern literary readers differ in handling the narrator's silence?
choices: Midrash ignores it; literary readers fill it
Both add new verses to the text
Midrash fills it with story; literary readers keep it and ask what it does
check.why: Midrash supplies motives and scenes; literary critics like Alter and Auerbach treat the gap itself as part of the art.

lessons.title: The Keyword
lessons.mainIdea: A repeated word, the keyword, can tie scenes together and carry a judgment the narrator never states.
reading: In the 1920s the German-Jewish thinkers Martin Buber and Franz Rosenzweig began a new German translation of the Bible. They noticed that Hebrew narrative repeats a single root word at key points, and they gave the device a name: *Leitwort*, leading word or *keyword*. The repetition is easy to miss in translation, because translators often vary their words for style. In Hebrew the same sound comes back, and a listener hears the thread. Buber and Rosenzweig tried to keep the repetitions in German so readers could hear them too.

Genesis 27 turns on such a thread. Jacob, dressed as Esau, receives the *blessing*, berakhah, meant for the firstborn. When Esau discovers the trick, he cries that his brother took his birthright, bekhorah, and now his blessing, berakhah. In Hebrew the two words share almost all their letters. The pun is Esau's, and it sums up the whole chapter: the two things Jacob took are, in sound, nearly one thing. Later in the story the word blessing keeps returning, when Jacob wrestles for one at the Jabbok and when he blesses his sons before he dies.

The sharpest example runs between two chapters. In Genesis 37 the brothers dip Joseph's coat in goat's blood and send it to their father with the words, in Hebrew, haker-na, "recognize, please," whether it is his son's coat. In Genesis 38, Judah, the brother who proposed selling Joseph, is handed his own seal, cord and staff by Tamar with the same two words: haker-na. Genesis Rabbah noticed the echo long ago and read it as measure for measure. Alter reads it the same way as a literary device. The narrator says nothing about justice; the keyword says it for him.

words.d: a word or root repeated at key points in a story to link scenes and carry meaning; Buber and Rosenzweig's Leitwort
berakhah in Hebrew, the spoken gift a father gives in Genesis; it drives the plot of Genesis 27
bekhorah, the firstborn's double share and standing, which Esau sells to Jacob for stew in Genesis 25
the idea, common in midrash, that a wrong is answered by a matching consequence

look.title: Recognize This
look.text: Genesis 37:32 (in summary): the brothers send Joseph's bloodied coat to Jacob and say, recognize now whether this is your son's coat. Jacob recognizes it and mourns. Genesis 38:25–26 (in summary): Tamar, accused by Judah, sends him his own seal, cord and staff and says, recognize now whose these are. Judah recognizes them and admits she is more in the right than he.
look.prompt: The same Hebrew words open both moments. What has Judah done in chapter 37, and what happens to him in chapter 38? What does the repeated word ask the reader to conclude?

check.q: Who coined the term Leitwort for the repeated keyword in Hebrew narrative?
check.why: Buber and Rosenzweig identified the device while making their German translation in the 1920s; Alter later used the idea in English.

check.q: Which two Hebrew words does Esau play on in Genesis 27?
check.why: Esau says Jacob took his birthright and now his blessing; the two words share nearly all their letters.

check.q: What links the coat scene in Genesis 37 with Tamar's scene in Genesis 38?
choices: The words haker-na, "recognize, please," open both
check.why: Judah's brothers tell Jacob to recognize the coat; Tamar tells Judah to recognize his own things; the echo is read as measure for measure.

lessons.title: The Meeting at the Well
lessons.mainIdea: Biblical narrative uses type-scenes, set patterns the audience knew, and tells character through how each telling changes the pattern.
reading: Three times in the Torah a man arrives at a well in a foreign land, meets a young woman, water is drawn, she runs home with the news, and a marriage follows. In Genesis 24 Abraham's servant meets Rebekah. In Genesis 29 Jacob meets Rachel. In Exodus 2 Moses meets the daughters of the priest of Midian. Alter called this a *type-scene*: a fixed pattern that an ancient audience would have recognized the moment a traveler reached a well, the way a modern audience knows what a first-date scene in a movie will do.

The art is in the variation. In Genesis 24 the servant is passive and prays; Rebekah does all the work, drawing water for ten camels, and the scene is long and formal. In Genesis 29 Jacob sees Rachel, rolls a heavy stone off the well's mouth by himself, waters her sheep, kisses her and weeps. The scene is quick and physical, and it shows a Jacob who acts before he thinks. In Exodus 2 Moses drives off the shepherds who are bullying the daughters, which fits the man who has just struck down an Egyptian taskmaster. Each hero is shown by how he handles the same scene.

Knowing the pattern also lets a reader notice when it is missing. Isaac never goes to a well; a servant goes for him, and Isaac is the most passive of the three patriarchs throughout Genesis. Later readers have used the type-scene to think about the women, who in each scene are the ones with water to give. The rabbis had their own way of linking these scenes, noting for example that wells follow the family from Abraham to the well of Miriam in the wilderness. The literary reader and the midrashic reader are both hearing a pattern; they describe it in different words.

words.d: a set narrative pattern, such as the meeting at a well, repeated with variations that reveal character
one of the founding fathers of Israel in Genesis: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
a region east of the Gulf of Aqaba where Moses flees and meets his wife in Exodus 2

look.title: Three Wells, Three Men
look.text: Genesis 24: Abraham's servant waits by a well and prays for a sign; Rebekah draws water for him and for all his camels; she runs home. Genesis 29: Jacob sees Rachel coming with her father's sheep, rolls the stone off the well alone, waters the flock, kisses her and weeps; she runs home. Exodus 2: Moses sits by a well; shepherds drive off the priest's daughters; Moses stands up for them and waters their flock; they run home.
look.prompt: Name the parts that stay the same. Then say what each variation shows about the man at the well and about the woman he meets.

check.q: What is a type-scene?
choices: A scene printed in a different typeface
A scene that appears only once in the Bible
A set narrative pattern told more than once with variations
A scene added by a later editor
check.why: Alter's term names a fixed pattern, like the meeting at the well, whose variations tell the reader about each character.

check.q: Which detail in Genesis 29 shows Jacob acting before he thinks?
choices: He rolls the stone off the well alone and kisses Rachel
check.why: Jacob's quick, physical actions at the well contrast with the servant's prayer in Genesis 24 and Moses' defense of the daughters in Exodus 2.

check.q: Which patriarch never has a well scene of his own, and what does that suggest?
choices: Isaac; he is the most passive of the three
check.why: A servant goes to the well for Isaac in Genesis 24, which fits the way Isaac is acted upon rather than acting throughout Genesis.

lessons.title: Two Sons and One Blessing
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 25–27 tells how Jacob gained Esau's birthright and blessing, and readers from Rashi to today have argued about what it means.
reading: Before the twins are born, Rebekah feels them struggling inside her and asks God why. The answer, in Genesis 25:23, is an oracle: two nations are in her womb, and the elder shall serve the younger. The reader knows this before either parent acts. Esau, the elder, comes home famished and sells his birthright to Jacob for bread and a stew of lentils. The text says he ate, drank, rose, went his way, and despised his birthright. Five verbs in a row, and one judgment: the narrator almost never judges, so this one counts.

In Genesis 27 Isaac is old and blind and asks Esau to hunt game and prepare a meal so he can bless him. Rebekah overhears and sends Jacob in with goat meat and goat skins on his arms and neck. Isaac is suspicious. He feels the hairy arms and says a line that Jewish tradition has quoted for centuries: the voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau. He blesses Jacob. When Esau returns, Isaac trembles, and Esau weeps and asks whether there is no blessing left for him. He receives a lesser one. He plans to kill his brother, and Jacob flees.

Readers have handled the deception in many ways. Rashi, following the midrash, softens Jacob's lie by reading his words "I am Esau thy firstborn" as two statements: I am the one bringing you food; Esau is your firstborn. Rabbinic tradition also came to read Esau as Edom and later as Rome, so his loss became a story about nations. Ramban and others admit the plain sense: Jacob deceived his father. Many modern readers, Jewish and otherwise, point out that the story itself answers the deception. Jacob will be deceived in the dark by Laban, who gives him the elder sister when he expected the younger. The text does not say this is justice. It only tells both stories and lets the reader hear the echo.

words.d: a message from God given in answer to a question, such as the one Rebekah receives about her twins in Genesis 25:23
Jacob's elder twin, a hunter, whom later tradition identifies with the nation of Edom
the nation south-east of the Dead Sea that Genesis 36 traces to Esau; rabbinic tradition later used the name for Rome

look.title: The Voice and the Hands
look.text: The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.
look.prompt: Isaac has evidence on both sides. What does he choose to trust, and what might the narrator be showing about how deception works?

check.q: What does the oracle in Genesis 25:23 tell Rebekah?
choices: That she will have twelve sons
That the elder of the two nations in her womb shall serve the younger
That her husband will go blind
That she must return to Haran
check.why: The oracle announces two nations and the elder serving the younger; this shapes how readers view what follows.

check.q: How does Rashi handle Jacob's words "I am Esau thy firstborn"?
choices: He says Jacob never spoke them
He reads them as two statements: I am the one bringing food; Esau is your firstborn
He says they were spoken by Rebekah
check.why: Rashi, following midrash, splits the sentence to lessen the lie; Ramban and modern readers accept the plain sense that Jacob deceived his father.

check.q: Which later event do many readers hear as an echo of Jacob's deception of Isaac?
choices: Laban giving Jacob the elder sister in the dark
check.why: Jacob, who took the elder's place by deceiving a blind father, is himself deceived in the dark about which sister he has married.

lessons.title: Leah and Rachel
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 29–30 gives the sisters voices through the names they give their sons, and their story shaped later Jewish memory.
reading: Jacob works seven years for Rachel, and the text says they seemed to him a few days because of his love. On the wedding night Laban brings him Leah, the elder sister, and in the morning, the text says, behold, it was *Leah*. When Jacob protests, Laban answers that in his place the younger is not given before the firstborn. The reader who remembers Genesis 27 hears the word firstborn land. Jacob works seven more years for *Rachel*. Now he has two wives who are sisters, and the text says he loved Rachel more.

The narrator gives the sisters almost no description beyond a line about Leah's eyes and Rachel's beauty. Their inner lives come through the names they give their children. Leah names her first son Reuben and explains it: the LORD has seen her affliction, and now her husband will love her. Simeon: the LORD heard she was hated. Levi: now her husband will be joined to her. Judah: this time she will praise the LORD. Four births, four short speeches, and a whole marriage told from inside. Rachel, childless, says to Jacob, give me children, or else I die. Jacob answers in anger.

Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin on the road near Bethlehem, and Jacob sets a pillar on her grave. Centuries later the prophet Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping for her children as they go into exile, and God answering that they will return. The passage, Jeremiah 31:15 in many Bibles and 31:14 in the Hebrew numbering, is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah. Rachel's tomb near Bethlehem became a place of Jewish prayer. Leah, the less loved, is buried with Jacob in the cave of Machpelah. The narrator does not say which sister the story favors. Rabbinic readers noted that Leah is the mother of Judah and Levi, the lines of kings and priests, and that Rachel is the mother of Joseph. Modern readers have found in the sisters a study of love, envy and being unseen.

words.d: Laban's elder daughter, Jacob's first wife, mother of six of his sons and of Dinah
Laban's younger daughter, whom Jacob loved; mother of Joseph and Benjamin, buried near Bethlehem
the cave at Hebron that Abraham bought in Genesis 23; Genesis names it as the burial place of the patriarchs and of Sarah, Rebekah and Leah

look.title: Four Names, One Marriage
look.text: Genesis 29:31–35 (in summary): Leah names her sons and gives a reason for each. Reuben: because the LORD has looked on my affliction; now my husband will love me. Simeon: because the LORD heard that I am hated. Levi: now my husband will be joined to me. Judah: this time I will praise the LORD. The narrator adds no comment on any of the four.
look.prompt: Read the four reasons in order. What changes between the first name and the last? What does the reader learn about Leah that the narrator never says directly?

check.q: How does the text let the reader inside Leah's feelings?
choices: Through the names and reasons she gives her sons
Through a long speech to Jacob
Through the narrator's description of her thoughts
Through a letter to her father
check.why: Genesis 29:31–35 gives Leah four naming speeches; the narrator adds nothing, so the names carry her inner life.

check.q: What does Laban say when Jacob protests that he was given Leah?
choices: That in his place the younger is not given before the firstborn
That the seven years were not finished
check.why: Laban's answer uses the word firstborn, which many readers hear as an echo of Jacob taking the elder's place in Genesis 27.

check.q: Where does the prophet Jeremiah picture Rachel, and why is the passage important in Jewish practice?
choices: In Egypt, blessing Joseph; it is read on Passover
At the Jabbok, wrestling; it is read at weddings
Weeping for her children going into exile; it is read on Rosh Hashanah
In Eden, naming the animals; it is read on Shabbat
check.why: Jeremiah 31 pictures Rachel weeping and God promising return; the passage is the prophetic reading on the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

lessons.title: The Night at the Jabbok
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 32 tells of a night wrestling match that ends in a wound, a blessing and the name Israel, and readers have never agreed on who the stranger was.
reading: Twenty years after fleeing, Jacob heads home with two wives, eleven sons, a daughter and large flocks. Messengers report that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob divides his camp, prays, and sends waves of gifts ahead. That night he sends everyone across the *Jabbok* and stays alone. The text says a man wrestled with him until daybreak. The stranger wrenches Jacob's hip and asks to be released. Jacob demands a blessing. The stranger renames him *Israel*, and the text explains the name with the verb for striving: he has striven with God and with men and prevailed.

Jacob asks the stranger's name and is refused. He names the place *Peniel*, saying he has seen God face to face and lived. The sun rises as he crosses, limping. The text adds that for this reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew of the hip, a rule Jewish law still keeps. Then, in Genesis 33, Esau runs to meet him, embraces him and weeps, and the two brothers part in peace. The night's fight and the morning's meeting sit side by side, and the text does not explain how one led to the other.

Who was the man? Hosea 12 says Jacob strove with an angel. Genesis Rabbah, and Rashi after it, identifies the angel as the guardian angel of Esau, so that the night fight is a preview of the morning's meeting and of Israel's long struggle with Edom. Ramban reads the episode as a sign of future generations who will be wounded but not destroyed. Modern readers, Jewish and others, have seen Jacob wrestling with his own past, his guilt, or God directly. Alter notes the wordplay: Jacob (Ya'akov) at the Jabbok (Yabbok) wrestles (ye'avek). Every reading has to account for the limp. Jacob leaves with a new name, and he leaves marked.

words.d: a stream east of the Jordan where Jacob wrestles in Genesis 32; its Hebrew name sounds like Jacob's and like the word for wrestling
the name given to Jacob at the Jabbok, explained by the verb for striving; later the name of his descendants and their nation
"face of God," the name Jacob gives the place where he wrestled, saying he saw God face to face

look.title: A New Name
look.text: And he said: 'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed.'
look.cite: Genesis 32:29 (32:28 in Christian numbering), Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917
look.prompt: The name Jacob was explained at birth by his grip on Esau's heel. What does the new name say about him, and what does the limp add?

check.q: Which prophet identifies Jacob's opponent at the Jabbok as an angel?
check.why: Hosea 12 recalls Jacob striving with an angel; Genesis itself calls the opponent only a man.

check.q: How do Genesis Rabbah and Rashi identify the stranger?
choices: As the guardian angel of Esau
As the angel who stopped the Akedah
check.why: The midrash and Rashi read the fight as a struggle with Esau's angel, linking the night to the meeting with Esau the next morning.

check.q: What practice does Genesis 32 connect to the wrestling?
choices: Fasting on the ninth of Av
Not eating the sinew of the hip
check.why: The text says the children of Israel do not eat the hip sinew because Jacob's hip was struck; Jewish law keeps the rule.

lessons.title: Dinah's Chapter
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 34 tells a hard story in which Dinah never speaks, and readers across the centuries have argued about her brothers' violence.
reading: Genesis 34 is a chapter many teachers approach carefully. Dinah, Leah's daughter, goes out to see the women of the land. Shechem, a local prince, takes her by force, then wants to marry her. Her brothers, angry, tell Shechem's people that a marriage is possible only if all their men are circumcised. The men agree. While they are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill them all and take Dinah from Shechem's house. Jacob says they have brought trouble on him. The brothers answer with the last words of the chapter: should our sister be treated as a harlot? The narrator does not reply.

What the chapter leaves out is as striking as what it tells. Dinah does not speak a single word. The text does not say what she wanted, felt or suffered afterward. The gap is total. Jewish readers have argued for centuries about the brothers. Maimonides, in his law code, held that the people of Shechem were liable because they failed to bring Shechem to justice. Ramban disagreed sharply, arguing that Jacob's rebuke, repeated on his deathbed in Genesis 49, shows the killing was wrong. Both are reading the same silent chapter and the same words of Jacob.

On his deathbed, Jacob curses the anger of Simeon and Levi and scatters their tribes. Later readers have used this to argue that the text itself rejects the brothers' act, while others note that the brothers get the last word in chapter 34. Modern readers, especially women, have asked why Dinah is silent and have written to give her a voice, as Anita Diamant did in her 1997 novel The Red Tent. In a public school, the chapter is read as a text about violence, honor and a family, with its readers named. It is not read as a verdict on any people, then or now.

words.d: the daughter of Jacob and Leah, whose story in Genesis 34 is told without a single word from her
both a city in the hill country and the prince of Genesis 34 who takes Dinah
Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, or Rambam (1138–1204), philosopher and author of the law code Mishneh Torah

look.title: Two Legal Readers of Genesis 34
look.text: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 9:14 (in summary): the people of Shechem were liable because they saw the wrong done and did not bring the wrongdoer to judgment. Ramban on Genesis 34:13 (in summary): that cannot be right, because Jacob rebuked Simeon and Levi at once and cursed their anger years later; if the killing were just, Jacob would not have condemned it.
look.prompt: What evidence does each reader use? One reads the law; the other reads Jacob's words. Which parts of the chapter does each leave out?

check.q: What is most striking about Dinah's role in Genesis 34?
choices: She leads the attack on the city
She marries Shechem at the end
She never speaks a word in the chapter
check.why: The chapter carries her name but gives her no speech; the silence has been noticed by readers from the rabbis to modern novelists.

check.q: What does Ramban point to in arguing that the brothers' killing was wrong?
choices: Jacob's rebuke, repeated on his deathbed in Genesis 49
check.why: Ramban argues that Jacob's condemnation, at once and again in his final blessings, shows the text does not approve the act; Maimonides reads the case under law instead.

check.q: How should a class in a public school read a chapter like Genesis 34?
choices: As a text about violence and a family, with its readers named and no verdict on any people
As proof about the character of a whole nation
As a chapter to skip because it is difficult
As a story with one settled meaning
check.why: The course reads hard passages factually, with their context and their readers, and never as a judgment on a tradition or a people.

lessons.title: Dreams, the Coat and the Pit
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 37 sets the Joseph story in motion with dreams told twice, a coat, a pit and a sale, and its seams have interested both rabbis and scholars.
reading: Genesis 37 opens with Joseph at seventeen, tending sheep with his brothers and bringing their father a bad report of them. Jacob loves him more than the others and makes him a special coat, which JPS 1917 calls a coat of many colours; the Hebrew, ketonet passim, is uncertain, and some translations say a long-sleeved tunic. The brothers hate him. Then Joseph tells a *dream*: their sheaves bow to his. He tells another: the sun, moon and eleven stars bow to him. The brothers hate him more; his father rebukes him but, the text says, keeps the matter in mind.

Jacob sends Joseph to check on his brothers at Shechem. They see him coming and plan to kill him. Reuben, the eldest, persuades them to throw him into a pit instead, meaning to rescue him later. They strip the coat and put him in the pit. Then Judah proposes selling him to a passing caravan of Ishmaelites. The next verse says Midianite merchants pulled Joseph out and sold him to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt. When Reuben returns, the pit is empty and he tears his clothes. The brothers dip the coat in goat's blood and send it to their father.

Readers have noticed the seams. Who sold Joseph, the brothers, the Midianites or the Ishmaelites? Rashi works to make it one story, with several sales in a row. Rashbam, Rashi's grandson, reads the plain sense: the Midianites found Joseph and sold him while the brothers were eating, so the brothers never sold him at all, which is why Reuben is surprised. Source critics take the doubled names as a sign that two versions were combined. The literary reader notes the repeated pairs: two dreams, two rescuers, two sets of merchants, and a goat's blood that answers the goat skins Jacob once wore to deceive his own father.

words.d: in the Joseph story, a message about the future that comes in pairs and needs an interpreter
traders descended from Ishmael in Genesis; one of the two groups named in the sale of Joseph
Rabbi Shmuel ben Meir (c. 1085–c. 1158), Rashi's grandson, a commentator devoted to the plain sense of the text

look.title: Joseph's Life in Numbers
look.prompt: How many years pass between the pit and the palace? What do the paired sevens suggest about how the story is built?

check.q: What do Joseph's two dreams in Genesis 37 have in common?
choices: Both show his family bowing to him
check.why: Sheaves bow in the first and sun, moon and stars in the second; the pair sets up the brothers' bowing in Egypt.

check.q: How does Rashbam read the sale of Joseph?
choices: The Midianites found him and sold him while the brothers were eating
check.why: Rashbam's plain-sense reading has the Midianites take Joseph from the pit, which explains Reuben's surprise; Rashi harmonizes the names into one chain of sales.

check.q: Which earlier deception does the goat's blood on the coat echo?
choices: Jacob wearing goat skins to deceive Isaac
check.why: Jacob deceived his blind father with goat skins; now his sons deceive him with a coat dipped in goat's blood, an echo readers have long noticed.

lessons.title: Prison and Palace
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 39–41 moves Joseph from a prison to Pharaoh's court through dreams, and shows repetition with variation at work.
reading: In Egypt Joseph is bought by Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, and rises to run his house. The text says the LORD was with him, a phrase it repeats. Potiphar's wife tries to seduce him; he refuses; she accuses him falsely, and he is thrown into prison. There too he rises, put in charge of the other prisoners. Two of Pharaoh's officers, the chief butler and the chief baker, have troubling dreams. Joseph asks whether interpretations do not belong to God, and then interprets: the butler will be restored, the baker hanged. Both come true. The butler forgets him for two years.

Then *Pharaoh* dreams: seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, seven full ears of grain swallowed by seven thin ones. His wise men cannot interpret. The butler remembers. Joseph is shaved and dressed and brought before the king. Pharaoh retells his dreams, and the retelling is not word for word: he adds that the thin cows were the worst he had ever seen, and that after eating the fat cows they looked no better. Alter and others point out that Hebrew narrative almost never repeats a speech exactly. The changes show Pharaoh's fear, and the reader is meant to compare.

Joseph gives the *interpretation* to God, as he did in prison, and reads the two dreams as one: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine. Then he goes beyond interpreting and proposes a plan, a manager to store grain. Pharaoh gives him the job. Joseph receives an Egyptian name, Zaphenath-paneah, an Egyptian wife, Asenath, and Pharaoh's ring. He is thirty. The boy in the pit is now second in Egypt, and the story is halfway done. Nothing in the chapter says why events fall as they do; Joseph will offer his own reading of that in Genesis 45 and 50.

words.d: the title of the king of Egypt; the Joseph story never gives his personal name
the explanation of a dream's meaning, which Joseph says belongs to God
the Egyptian officer who buys Joseph and later imprisons him on his wife's false charge

look.title: The Dream Told Twice
look.text: Genesis 41:1–4 (in summary, the narrator): seven fine, fat cows come up from the river and feed; seven ugly, lean cows come up after them and eat the fat ones. Genesis 41:17–21 (in summary, Pharaoh retelling): seven fat, fine cows; then seven poor, very ugly and lean cows, such as I never saw in all Egypt for badness; and when they had eaten the fat cows, no one could tell they had done so, for they were as ugly as before.
look.prompt: List what Pharaoh adds. What do the additions tell you about the man telling the dream, and why might the narrator want the reader to compare?

check.q: To whom does Joseph say interpretations belong, both in prison and before Pharaoh?
choices: To the wise men of Egypt
check.why: In Genesis 40 and 41 Joseph credits God with interpretation rather than himself, a point the text stresses twice.

check.q: What does Pharaoh's retelling of his dream add that the narrator's version did not include?
choices: That the thin cows looked no better after eating the fat ones
That the dream took place in a palace
check.why: Pharaoh adds his own fear to the retelling; Hebrew narrative repeats speeches with changes so the reader can compare.

check.q: What does Joseph do beyond interpreting Pharaoh's dreams?
choices: He asks to be sent home to Canaan
He demands the release of the baker
He proposes a plan to store grain and is given the job
check.why: Joseph moves from interpreter to adviser, proposing a manager for the years of plenty; Pharaoh appoints him and gives him a name, a wife and a ring.

lessons.title: Judah's Speech
lessons.mainIdea: Judah's speech in Genesis 44:18–34 is the longest in Genesis and the turning point of the story, and Jewish tradition reads it as a model of teshuvah.
reading: The famine brings Joseph's brothers to Egypt to buy grain. They do not recognize the Egyptian official who tests them harshly, holds Simeon, and demands they bring their youngest brother, *Benjamin*. Jacob refuses for a long time. Judah finally pledges himself as surety for the boy. On the second trip, Joseph hides his silver cup in Benjamin's sack, has the brothers arrested and announces that Benjamin alone will stay as his slave. The others may go home. It is exactly the situation of chapter 37, with a Rachel's son in danger and the brothers free to abandon him.

Judah steps forward and speaks. His speech, Genesis 44:18–34, runs seventeen verses, the longest single speech in Genesis. He retells the whole story from the brothers' side: the official asked about their family; they told him of an old father and a young brother whose brother is dead; the father said his soul is bound up with the boy's. Judah does not argue the law of the cup. He talks about a father. Then he offers himself as slave in place of Benjamin, because he cannot bear to see the grief that would come upon his father. At that, Joseph can no longer hold back.

The rabbis of the Talmud defined complete *teshuvah*, return or repentance, as coming to the same situation and choosing differently; Maimonides wrote this definition into his law code. Many Jewish readers see Judah's speech as its clearest picture in the Torah. The brother who once said, come, let us sell him, now says, take me instead. Literary readers point to the craft: the speech works by retelling, which lets the reader hear the brothers' story with new feeling, and it never once mentions Joseph's name. Jewish tradition also marks the moment. The weekly portion that begins at this verse is called Vayigash, and he drew near, from Judah's first word.

words.d: the youngest son of Jacob and Rachel's second son, whom Joseph tests the brothers over in Genesis 44
return or repentance; in rabbinic teaching, complete teshuvah means facing the same situation and choosing differently
"and he drew near," the weekly Torah portion beginning at Genesis 44:18 with Judah's speech
a person who pledges to bear the loss if another fails; Judah makes himself surety for Benjamin

look.title: Take Me Instead
look.text: Genesis 44:30–34 (in summary): Judah tells the Egyptian official that his father's life is bound up with the boy's life. If they return without him, the father will die of grief, and the brothers will have brought down his gray hairs to the grave. Judah says he became surety for the boy. So, he asks, let me stay as your slave in place of the lad, and let the lad go up with his brothers, for how can I go up to my father if the boy is not with me?
look.prompt: Compare this with Judah's proposal in Genesis 37:26–27. What has changed in the man? What does he never mention, and why might that matter?

check.q: What makes the situation in Genesis 44 a repeat of Genesis 37?
choices: The brothers are again in a pit
A son of Rachel is again in danger while the other brothers may walk away
check.why: Benjamin, Rachel's son, is to be enslaved while the others go free, mirroring the moment the brothers abandoned Joseph.

check.q: How did the rabbis define complete teshuvah, in a definition Maimonides later codified?
choices: Facing the same situation and choosing differently
check.why: The Talmud describes the penitent as one who meets the same temptation and refrains; readers see Judah's offer as the Torah's picture of this.

check.q: Which detail about Judah's speech do literary readers stress?
choices: It quotes the law of the stolen cup
It is the shortest speech in Genesis
It retells the story from the brothers' side and never names Joseph
check.why: The speech works by retelling with feeling and by centering the father; it is also the longest speech in Genesis, not the shortest.

lessons.title: The Recognition Scene
lessons.mainIdea: Joseph's revealing of himself in Genesis 45, and his words in Genesis 50, give the story its own reading of why things happened.
reading: Joseph sends every Egyptian from the room and weeps so loudly that the household hears. Then he says the words the brothers have not heard in twenty-two years of story time: I am Joseph. Is my father still alive? The brothers cannot answer. The text says they are dismayed at his presence. He tells them to come near, repeats his name, and adds that he is the brother they sold into Egypt. Then he tells them not to grieve, for God sent him ahead to preserve life. The scene the Greeks called *recognition*, the moment a hidden identity comes to light, is the hinge of the second half of Genesis.

Joseph offers an interpretation of his own life, and the narrator neither confirms nor denies it. Twice in chapter 45 and once more in chapter 50, after Jacob's death, Joseph says that what the brothers meant for evil, God meant for good, to keep many people alive. Jewish tradition has generally read the Joseph story through these words as a story of *providence*, God's guidance working through human choices. Literary readers note that this is the only place in the story where anyone explains the plot, and that the explanation comes from a character, not from the narrator. The reader decides how much weight it carries.

Genesis ends in Egypt. Jacob blesses his sons and is carried home to Machpelah for burial. Joseph dies at 110 and is embalmed, and the last verse leaves him in a coffin in Egypt, having made his brothers swear to carry his bones home when God brings them up from the land. The Torah's next book opens with those descendants enslaved. The German novelist Thomas Mann spent the years 1933 to 1943, the years of the Nazi rise and the war, writing Joseph and His Brothers, a four-volume retelling. A story of a family reconciled, ending in a coffin waiting to go home, has been read as many things. The text gives the coffin and the oath.

words.d: the scene in a story when a hidden identity is revealed, as when Joseph tells his brothers who he is
the idea that God guides events, including through human choices; the reading Joseph gives of his own story
German novelist (1875–1955) whose four-volume Joseph and His Brothers (1933–1943) retells Genesis 37–50

look.title: What You Meant and What God Meant
look.text: And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
look.prompt: This is Joseph's reading of his own story. Does the narrator ever say the same thing? What is the difference between a character's interpretation and the narrator's?

check.q: What are Joseph's first words when he reveals himself in Genesis 45?
choices: I am Joseph; is my father still alive?
Take me instead of the lad
check.why: Joseph's revelation begins with his name and a question about his father; the other lines belong to Genesis 37, 44 and 22.

check.q: Who in the story explains that God meant the events for good?
check.why: The explanation comes from Joseph in chapters 45 and 50; the narrator never states it, which literary readers point out.

check.q: How does the book of Genesis end?
choices: With the family returning to Canaan
With the giving of the Torah
With Joseph in a coffin in Egypt, after an oath to carry his bones home
check.why: Genesis 50:26 leaves Joseph embalmed in Egypt; Exodus opens with his descendants enslaved there.

lessons.title: As Literature and as Torah
lessons.mainIdea: The same chapters can be read as literature and as Torah, and knowing both ways of reading is the goal of this unit.
reading: Reading Genesis 25–50 as *literature* means asking how the text works: the narrator's economy, the keyword, the type-scene, repetition with variation, the gap that the reader must fill. It means treating Jacob, Leah and Judah as characters who change, and treating the writer, whoever that was, as an artist. Scholars like Alter, Meir Sternberg and Adele Berlin built this approach in the 1980s. It can be practiced by anyone, of any faith or none, and it is the way a public school can read the text together.

Reading the same chapters as Torah means reading them as Jewish tradition does: as sacred teaching, divided into weekly *parashot* and read aloud on Shabbat through the year, surrounded by commentary, argued over in study pairs, with rules of practice drawn from them, such as the sinew of the hip. Rabbinic tradition says the Torah has seventy faces, meaning that many readings can be true at once. In this way of reading, the gaps are not only art; they are invitations, and midrash is the tradition's answer. The plain sense, peshat, and the searching sense, *derash*, sit side by side on the same page.

The two ways are not enemies. Many Jewish scholars do both, and many literary readers learn from Rashi. Where they differ is in the question each asks. The literary reader asks what the text does. The reader of Torah asks what the text asks of the reader. A student in this course should be able to do the first, describe the second accurately, and say clearly which one is speaking at any moment. That skill, keeping the text, its readers and yourself distinct, is what close reading of Genesis has been teaching since Rashi's classroom in Troyes and long before.

words.d: writing read for its art, its form and its meaning; reading Genesis as literature asks how the text works
a weekly portion of the Torah read on Shabbat; plural parashot; Genesis has twelve
the searching or interpretive sense of a text, as in midrash, set beside peshat, the plain sense
the Jewish day of rest, when a portion of the Torah is read aloud in the synagogue

look.title: Where the Weekly Portions Begin
look.cite: The annual Torah reading cycle; standard chapter divisions
look.prompt: Seven portions cover twenty-six chapters. Which portions break inside a chapter rather than at its start? What might that show about how the tradition divides the story?

check.q: Which question belongs to reading Genesis as literature?
choices: What practice does this verse require?
How does the narrator use repetition here?
Which portion is read this Shabbat?
What does Rashi rule about the sinew?
check.why: The literary reader asks how the text works; questions about practice and the reading cycle belong to reading as Torah.

check.q: What does the saying that the Torah has seventy faces mean in rabbinic tradition?
choices: Many readings of a text can be true at once
The Torah was written in seventy languages
check.why: The phrase, found in Numbers Rabbah, expresses the tradition's openness to many interpretations of the same verse.

check.q: What is the difference between peshat and derash?
choices: Peshat is Aramaic; derash is Hebrew
Peshat is Rashi's method; derash is Alter's
Peshat is the law; derash is the story
Peshat is the plain sense; derash is the searching, interpretive sense
check.why: Peshat reads the text in its context and grammar; derash searches it for further meaning, as midrash does; both appear together in traditional study.

review.q: What did Robert Alter mean by the economy of biblical narrative?
choices: The text uses the fewest words needed and every detail counts
The text is about trade and money
The text was cheap to copy
review.why: Economy names the restraint of the narrator, who gives actions and speech and withholds feelings and judgments.

review.q: Which repeated Hebrew words tie Genesis 37 to Genesis 38?
review.why: The brothers tell Jacob to recognize the coat; Tamar tells Judah to recognize his own things; the keyword is read as measure for measure.

review.q: Which of these is a type-scene in the Torah?
choices: The meeting at a well that leads to a marriage
review.why: The meeting at the well recurs for Rebekah, Rachel and Zipporah, with variations that reveal each man's character.

review.q: What does Laban's answer about the firstborn in Genesis 29 echo?
choices: Jacob taking the elder brother's place in Genesis 27
review.why: Laban says the younger is not given before the firstborn; the word firstborn recalls the blessing Jacob took as the younger twin.

review.q: Which reading of the stranger at the Jabbok belongs to Genesis Rabbah and Rashi?
review.why: The midrash identifies the opponent as Esau's angel, tying the night's fight to the morning's meeting; the conscience reading is modern.

review.q: How do Maimonides and Ramban differ on Genesis 34?
choices: Maimonides says Dinah spoke; Ramban says she did not
Maimonides finds the city liable under law; Ramban says Jacob's rebuke shows the killing was wrong
Both say the chapter is a later addition
review.why: Maimonides reads the case in his law code; Ramban answers from Jacob's words in chapters 34 and 49; they disagree.

review.q: Why do many Jewish readers call Judah's speech in Genesis 44 a picture of teshuvah?
choices: Because Judah faces the same situation as in Genesis 37 and chooses differently
review.why: The rabbinic definition of complete teshuvah is choosing differently in the same situation; Judah, who once sold a brother, now offers himself in place of one.

review.q: Who states, within the story, that God meant the brothers' evil for good?
review.why: Joseph gives this reading in Genesis 45 and 50; the narrator never states it, so the reader weighs a character's interpretation.
